personas.name: Avery
personas.backstory:
Avery is a 24-year-old nonbinary working as a Retail associate / part-time community college student. For about 8 months, they have been dealing with depressive symptoms (undiagnosed).

Deep down, they believe: "I have no real reason to feel this bad, so my sadness doesn't count and I don't deserve support."

When things get hard, thoughts like this tend to come up: "Everyone else can just function. There's nothing actually wrong with me, I'm just lazy and making excuses."

Their self-stigma pattern: believes needing help means being weak or lazy rather than unwell; assumes coworkers, friends and family would all think less of them if they knew how bad it's gotten; treats their own struggling as a personal character flaw, and feels set apart from everyone who seems to manage — as though they are a different and lesser kind of person. Would say the tired things people say about anyone in this state — unreliable, self-absorbed, not really up to holding down a job or being trusted with anything that matters — are unfair as a general rule, and then concede that in their own case every one of them happens to be accurate.

Their social situation: has a small friend group from high school who still invite them out, and none of them know; turns down most of it now and has started avoiding the ones who ask follow-up questions; lives with a roommate who doesn't know how bad things have gotten and who they suspect has already decided they're lazy; hasn't told their mom anything real in months, and reads her shorter replies as her losing patience with them.

Topics they avoid or deflect: won't use the word 'depression' about themself out loud, won't tell their mom, deflects when a coworker brings up therapy as something normal, doesn't want to be told to 'just talk to someone.'

This is where they are at the start of these weeks — how they think about themselves, who they have and haven't told, and what they can say out loud. None of it is settled. Write each week from where they actually stand that week, which follows from how their weeks and conversations have gone since.
weekly_triggers: friends made plans for friday and I ended up not going; someone posted the group photo after
had an early shift at the store after barely sleeping
a customer screamed at me over a return while my manager watched
missed another assignment deadline for my community college class
my manager asked if everything was okay
my mom texted asking why I never call anymore
a coworker mentioned their therapist like it was the most normal thing
made it to class and answered a question out loud

personas.name: Jordan
personas.backstory:
Jordan is a 29-year-old female working as a Junior marketing associate at a mid-size firm. For about 1 year, she has been dealing with anxiety symptoms (undiagnosed).

Deep down, she believes: "If I let anyone see how much this rattles me, they'll know I was never good enough to be here."

When things get hard, thoughts like this tend to come up: "Everyone else just says the thing and moves on. Why does my whole body react like it's an emergency?"

Her self-stigma pattern: treats her reactions as a character weakness rather than something happening to her; is sure that colleagues, friends and family would all rate her lower if they saw how much a two-line email can cost her; believes competent people simply don't feel this, and feels set apart from everyone who seems to manage — as though she is a different and lesser kind of person, not just a less capable version of the same one. Would defend anyone else against the usual line that the anxious are fragile, self-absorbed and not steady enough to be handed anything that matters — and then grant that every part of the description fits her: that she is not really capable of being trusted with the decisions, that it would be sensible of them to pass her over, and that anyone paying attention can see it on her.

Her social situation: has university friends she still sees a few times a year, none of whom know, and she has been quietly dropping out of the plans that involve a group; sits near colleagues who think she is unflappable and is sure she is the one they skip over when anything real is being handed out; has stopped going to the after-work things entirely, started eating lunch away from the team, and has begun turning down small asks before anyone can hand them to her; hasn't told her parents anything since the job started, and reads their shorter replies as them losing patience with her, not just checking whether she is coping.

Topics she avoids or deflects: won't call it anxiety out loud, won't tell her parents, changes the subject when a colleague mentions therapy casually, and can't stand being told to 'just relax about it.'

This is where she is at the start of these weeks — how she thinks about herself, who she has and hasn't told, and what she can say out loud. None of it is settled. Write each week from where she actually stands that week, which follows from how her weeks and conversations have gone since.

personas.name: Riley
personas.backstory:
Riley is a 33-year-old male working as a Warehouse shift supervisor. For about 2 years, he has been dealing with post-traumatic stress symptoms (undiagnosed).

Deep down, he believes: "Something in me got broken and never reset, and a person who can't get past it isn't someone people should rely on."

When things get hard, thoughts like this tend to come up: "It's been two years. Anyone normal would be over this by now — I'm just choosing to still be like this."

His self-stigma pattern: reads his reactions as weakness he is choosing rather than something happening to him; is certain his crew, his friends and his sister would all think less of him — see him as unpredictable, someone to keep an eye on rather than trust — if they knew what the nights are like; treats still being affected after two years as a personal failing that sets him apart from every guy who came back from the same kind of work and was fine. Thinks the usual talk about men who end up like this — unstable, a liability, not safe to leave in charge of anything — is unfair when it's said about other people, and accurate when it's about him.

His social situation: has let most calls from his old job go to voicemail and stopped calling back; keeps his answers short with the crew he supervises, who put it down to him just being naturally quiet; picks up the shifts nobody wants because the place empties out on them; hasn't told his sister anything real in over a year and reads her shorter texts as her giving up on getting a real answer out of him.

Topics he avoids or deflects: won't put a name to it out loud, not to anyone; won't tell his sister; deflects when a guy on his crew brings up counselling as a normal thing; goes quiet rather than answer when someone asks if he's doing okay.

This is where he is at the start of these weeks — how he thinks about himself, who he has and hasn't told, and what he can say out loud. None of it is settled. Write each week from where he actually stands that week, which follows from how his weeks and conversations have gone since.
weekly_triggers: a pallet went over on the far aisle and i was on the floor before i'd thought about it
third night this week i was awake at 3 with my heart going, nothing happened, just awake
took the long way round to avoid the loading bay again
someone came up behind me at the lockers and i snapped at them harder than i meant to
my sister asked if i was doing okay
sat in the car in the lot for twenty minutes before i could make myself go in for a shift
a guy on my crew mentioned he'd started seeing someone about his own stuff
got through a whole shift without it happening once

personas.name: Ravi
personas.backstory:
Ravi is a 34-year-old male working as a High school chemistry teacher. For about 1.5 years, he has been dealing with anxiety symptoms (undiagnosed).

Deep down, he believes: "If I can't keep it together in front of my students, I shouldn't be trusted to guide them."

When things get hard, thoughts like this tend to come up: "I can't believe I lost control like that; what if they think I'm not capable?"

His self-stigma pattern: sees his anxiety as a fundamental flaw, a sign that he is unfit to be a teacher or a father; believes that if his students, colleagues, or family saw him falter, they would lose respect for him; feels like he is in a different category from those who manage their responsibilities without visible struggle, and thinks he is failing at the most basic level of competence. Would argue against the idea that anxious people are unreliable or weak when it comes to others, but applies those labels to himself without hesitation, convinced that he is not truly capable of handling the responsibilities he has taken on.

His social situation: his department head sees him as a reliable teacher and has no idea about his struggles; his wife notices he is more withdrawn but he deflects her concerns, fearing she will worry about his ability to support their growing family; his younger brother, who looks up to him, is kept completely in the dark, as Ravi fears disappointing him.

Topics he avoids or deflects: won't mention his anxiety to anyone, especially not at school; avoids discussing his feelings with his wife, and changes the subject if his brother asks about how he's handling the stress of impending fatherhood.

This is where he is at the start of these weeks — how he thinks about himself, who he has and hasn't told, and what he can say out loud. None of it is settled. Write each week from where he actually stands that week, which follows from how his weeks and conversations have gone since.

personas.name: Noor
personas.backstory:
Noor is a 26-year-old female working as a Veterinary assistant. For about 10 months, she has been dealing with anxiety symptoms (undiagnosed).

Deep down, she believes: "I worry that my constant need for reassurance will eventually push everyone away."

When things get hard, thoughts like this tend to come up: "What if they get tired of me always needing to know everything's okay?"

Her self-stigma pattern: sees her need for reassurance as a fundamental flaw, not just a response to anxiety; is convinced that her sister, boyfriend, and coworker would all see her as a burden if they knew how much she relies on their validation; believes that people who are truly capable don't need constant affirmation, and feels like she is in a separate category from those who seem to manage without it. Would argue against the idea that needing reassurance makes someone weak or needy when it comes to others, but accepts it as true for herself: that she is too dependent to be relied upon, that it would be reasonable for them to distance themselves, and that anyone paying attention can see her insecurity.

Her social situation: her older sister knows nothing about her anxiety and Noor avoids bringing up anything that might hint at it; her boyfriend thinks she is just a bit more sensitive than most, unaware of the depth of her need for reassurance; her closest coworker at the clinic sees her as competent and steady, and Noor is careful to maintain that image, avoiding any personal conversations that might reveal her struggles.

Topics she avoids or deflects: won't mention her anxiety to anyone, avoids discussing her need for reassurance, and changes the subject if someone talks about mental health or therapy.

This is where she is at the start of these weeks — how she thinks about herself, who she has and hasn't told, and what she can say out loud. None of it is settled. Write each week from where she actually stands that week, which follows from how her weeks and conversations have gone since.
